mcp-initialize.title: initialize handshake returns serverInfo + protocolVersion
mcp-initialize.goal: Answer JSON-RPC initialize with serverInfo and protocolVersion so clients can begin a session
mcp-initialize.fix:
Answer the JSON-RPC `initialize` method on your MCP endpoint with a `result` that carries
`serverInfo` (an object with `name` and `version`) and `protocolVersion`. Accept `POST` with
`Content-Type: application/json` and `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`, and echo
the negotiated `protocolVersion` (the current pinned value is `2025-06-18`).

mcp-capabilities.title: initialize advertises capabilities
mcp-capabilities.goal: Advertise the capability groups your MCP server implements in the initialize result
mcp-capabilities.fix:
Populate the `capabilities` object in your `initialize` result. Clients gate feature use on
it: an empty or missing `capabilities` tells a client nothing is available, so it will not
call `tools/list`, `resources/list`, or `prompts/list`. Advertise the groups your server
actually implements (for example `{ "tools": {} }`).

mcp-tools-list.title: tools/list returns a tools array with input schemas
mcp-tools-list.goal: Return tools/list entries with name, description, and a JSON inputSchema
mcp-tools-list.fix:
Return `result.tools` as an array from the `tools/list` method. Each tool needs a `name`, a
`description`, and a JSON Schema `inputSchema` so an agent can validate arguments before
calling. A tool without an `inputSchema` forces the agent to guess argument shapes.

mcp-resources-list.title: resources/list returns at least one resource when advertised
mcp-resources-list.goal: Honor capabilities.resources with a non-empty resources/list result
mcp-resources-list.fix:
If `initialize` advertises `capabilities.resources`, implement `resources/list` and return a
`result.resources` array with at least one entry (`uri` plus a name or description). An empty
list or a transport failure means the capability was advertised but is not actually there.
Omit `capabilities.resources` entirely if the server has no resources.

mcp-modern-tools-list.title: header-routed tools/list (2026-07-28) returns tools without initialize
mcp-modern-tools-list.goal: Answer a modern header-routed tools/list without requiring an initialize handshake
mcp-modern-tools-list.fix:
Serve the modern MCP era (protocol revision `2026-07-28`): answer a `POST` whose headers
carry `MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28` and `Mcp-Method: tools/list` with a `result.tools`
array, with no prior `initialize` or `notifications/initialized`. Modern requests are
per-request enveloped: `params._meta` carries `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`,
`io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`, and `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`.
The `clientCapabilities` key is mandatory on every modern request; reject a request that
omits it with a well-formed `-32602`. `Mcp-Name` rides only `tools/call` (the tool name)
and `resources/read` (the resource URI), never `tools/list`.

mcp-server-discover.title: server/discover answers with server identity on the modern lane
mcp-server-discover.goal: Answer server/discover with supported versions, capabilities, and server identity
mcp-server-discover.fix:
Implement `server/discover` (protocol revision `2026-07-28`): return a result carrying
`supportedVersions` (the modern revisions you serve) and your advertised `capabilities`,
and identify the server in the result's `_meta` under
`io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo` (`name` plus `version`). The request arrives
header-routed (`MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28`, `Mcp-Method: server/discover`) with the
`params._meta` envelope, whose `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` key is
mandatory. No `initialize` precedes it: `server/discover` is how a modern client learns
what the server offers before any session state exists. Answering it is also what brings
the rest of the modern-lane checks into scoring, so serve the `2026-07-28` revision behind
it rather than this one method on its own.

mcp-unknown-method.title: unknown JSON-RPC method returns -32601
mcp-unknown-method.goal: Reject unknown JSON-RPC methods with error -32601 instead of a hang or 500
mcp-unknown-method.fix:
Reject an unknown JSON-RPC method with the standard error code `-32601` (Method not found),
not a hang, a 500, or a silent empty body. Agents rely on `-32601` to distinguish
"unsupported" from "failed"; anything else looks like an outage.

mcp-malformed-body.title: a non-JSON body draws -32700 (or a typed HTTP 400/415 refusal)
mcp-malformed-body.goal: Refuse an unparseable request body with a parse-error envelope or a typed HTTP refusal
mcp-malformed-body.fix:
Answer a `POST` whose body is not valid JSON with the JSON-RPC parse-error envelope
(`error.code: -32700`, `id: null`); delivering it at HTTP `400` is fine. A bare HTTP `400`
or `415` with no envelope also conforms as a typed refusal. What fails the check: a `200`
with garbage, a hang, or any other bare status (a bare `404` reads as a dead endpoint, not
a refusal).

mcp-batch-reject.title: a batch carrying a modern-envelope request is rejected -32600
mcp-batch-reject.goal: Refuse JSON array batches that carry modern-era envelopes with -32600
mcp-batch-reject.fix:
Reject a JSON array batch whose element carries the modern `params._meta` envelope
(protocol revision `2026-07-28`) with `error.code: -32600` (Invalid Request) and `id: null`.
Modern-era requests are single-request only: an envelope-bearing element inside an array is
never valid, so serving it (or answering anything other than `-32600`) is non-conforming.

mcp-unknown-tool.title: tools/call with an unknown tool name returns -32602
mcp-unknown-tool.goal: Reject an unknown tool name with -32602 instead of a hang, a 500, or a fake result
mcp-unknown-tool.fix:
Answer a `tools/call` whose `params.name` matches no registered tool with
`error.code: -32602` (Invalid params). Agents rely on the code to distinguish "no such
tool" from a transport failure; a hang, a `500`, or a `200` result for a tool that does
not exist all read as a broken server.

mcp-modern-unknown-method.title: an unknown method on the modern lane returns -32601
mcp-modern-unknown-method.goal: Reject unknown header-routed methods with -32601 on the 2026-07-28 lane
mcp-modern-unknown-method.fix:
Reject a modern request (`MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28`, `Mcp-Method` naming a method
you do not implement) with `error.code: -32601` (Method not found). Delivering the envelope
at HTTP `404` conforms; a bare `404` with no envelope does not (it is indistinguishable
from a dead endpoint).

mcp-modern-clientcaps.title: _meta missing clientCapabilities is rejected (-32602 or -32600)
mcp-modern-clientcaps.goal: Enforce the mandatory clientCapabilities key on every modern request
mcp-modern-clientcaps.fix:
Reject a modern request whose `params._meta` omits
`io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` with a well-formed error envelope. The check
accepts two codes: `-32602` (Invalid params, the SDK-typed refusal) as the primary, and
`-32600` (Invalid Request family) from conforming non-SDK servers. The key is mandatory on
every `2026-07-28` request even when the client has no capabilities to declare; an empty
object is valid.

mcp-modern-header-mismatch.title: an Mcp-Method header disagreeing with the body method draws -32020
mcp-modern-header-mismatch.goal: Validate the SEP-2243 header mirror between Mcp-Method and the body method
mcp-modern-header-mismatch.fix:
Reject a request whose `Mcp-Method` header names a different method than the JSON-RPC body
with `error.code: -32020` (header mismatch). The SEP-2243 headers exist so infrastructure
can route without parsing bodies; a disagreeing pair means the routing layer and the
handler would act on different methods, so it must be refused rather than silently
resolved in either direction.

mcp-modern-version-reject.title: an unsupported protocol version is rejected -32022 with data.supported
mcp-modern-version-reject.goal: Refuse unsupported protocol version claims with -32022 and advertise the served revisions
mcp-modern-version-reject.fix:
Reject a request claiming an unsupported `MCP-Protocol-Version` with
`error.code: -32022` (UnsupportedProtocolVersion) and populate `error.data.supported` with
the revisions you serve (for example `["2026-07-28"]`); echoing the claim in
`error.data.requested` helps debugging. The `data.supported` array is what lets a typed
client fall back to a revision you both speak, so an envelope without it fails the check.

mcp-modern-resources-miss.title: modern resources/read with an unknown URI returns -32602
mcp-modern-resources-miss.goal: Answer an unknown resource URI with the typed miss code, not a hang or a fake result
mcp-modern-resources-miss.fix:
Answer a modern `resources/read` (with `Mcp-Name` mirroring `params.uri`) for a URI that
matches no resource with `error.code: -32602`. That is the code current SDK lines put on
the wire for a resource miss; `-32002` (the legacy resource-not-found code) is also
tolerated from non-SDK servers. A hang, a `500`, or a fabricated `200` result fails. This
check only runs when the server advertises resources on either era lane.

mcp-accept-json.title: a JSON-only Accept is answered without SSE framing
mcp-accept-json.goal: Serve a single application/json response to a client whose Accept names only application/json
mcp-accept-json.fix:
Read the request `Accept` header and answer within it. Streamable HTTP lets the server reply
either with one `application/json` body or with a `text/event-stream`, and the choice is the
client's to constrain: a caller that sends `Accept: application/json` alone is telling you its
HTTP client cannot read a stream. Answering that caller with `text/event-stream` returns a
`200` over a body it cannot parse, and no status code tells it what went wrong.
Parse the header with q-value semantics rather than a substring match, buffer the response,
and emit `Content-Type: application/json`. Reserve the stream for callers that accept it. If
your server genuinely cannot produce a single JSON body, refuse with `406 Not Acceptable`
instead: that at least fails the caller immediately and in the open.

mcp-accept-unsatisfiable.title: an unsatisfiable Accept draws a 406 rather than an unasked-for type
mcp-accept-unsatisfiable.goal: Refuse an Accept you cannot satisfy with 406, never a 200 carrying a type the client did not request
mcp-accept-unsatisfiable.fix:
When the request `Accept` allows neither `application/json` nor `text/event-stream`, refuse
with `406 Not Acceptable` before any JSON-RPC parsing runs. Those two media types are the
whole of what the streamable-HTTP transport is defined over, so an `Accept` naming neither
cannot be served.
The failure this check looks for is a server that ignores `Accept` and answers with its one
representation under a success status, leaving the caller to sniff the body to find out the
negotiation never happened. Worse is a `200` that echoes the requested type back in
`Content-Type` while carrying a JSON-RPC body: the caller routes on your label and the parse
fails downstream.
Do the check at the transport edge and keep the body plain text, so no client mistakes the
refusal for a JSON-RPC error envelope.

mcp-get-fast-fail.title: GET on the MCP endpoint answers fast
mcp-get-fast-fail.goal: Answer GET with 405 or an SSE stream, never a document and never a held-open hang
mcp-get-fast-fail.fix:
Answer a `GET` on the MCP endpoint promptly, and answer it as streamable HTTP defines.
The probe sends `Accept: text/event-stream`. A `200` whose `Content-Type` is `text/html`,
`text/markdown`, or any other non-SSE type fails: a catalog client treats that document as a
transport error. Return one of two answers. Fast-fail at the router with `405 Method Not
Allowed`, `Allow: POST`, and `Cache-Control: no-store`. Or return `200` with
`Content-Type: text/event-stream` and an SSE body. Put the human-readable description on a
different path. A held-open connection and a `5xx` also fail. A `408` or `429` asks to be
retried and is not scored.

mcp-cors-preflight.title: CORS preflight succeeds with Access-Control-Allow-* headers
mcp-cors-preflight.goal: Serve one consistent CORS posture on the MCP endpoint, full preflight support or none
mcp-cors-preflight.fix:
The audit scores CORS posture, not presence. Omitting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` from
both the `OPTIONS` preflight and the `POST` response is a consistent no-CORS posture (a
server-to-agent-only endpoint) and scores `n_a` with no penalty. This check fails only when
the posture is partial or misconfigured: the preflight carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
on a non-2xx response, or the `POST` carries it while the preflight does not. To support
browser-origin agents, answer the preflight with `204` (or `200`) plus
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and
`Access-Control-Allow-Headers`, and mirror `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the `POST`
response. To stay no-CORS, strip the headers from both surfaces.

mcp-cors-actual.title: POST response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin
mcp-cors-actual.goal: Mirror the declared CORS posture on the actual MCP POST response
mcp-cors-actual.fix:
Echo `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the actual `POST` response whenever the preflight
declares CORS: a browser blocks the response body when the header is absent even though the
preflight passed. Omitting the header from both the preflight and the `POST` is a consistent
no-CORS posture and scores `n_a` with no penalty; this check fails when the preflight
declares CORS but the `POST` omits the header.

mcp-server-card.title: An MCP server card is published
mcp-server-card.goal: Publish a SEP-2127 server card for your MCP server and list it in your AI catalog
mcp-server-card.fix:
Serve a SEP-2127 server card at `<endpoint>/server-card` (`/mcp/server-card` for an endpoint at
`/mcp`) as `application/mcp-server-card+json`. It carries `$schema`
(`https://static.modelcontextprotocol.io/schemas/v1/server-card.schema.json`), `name` in reverse-DNS
form (`com.example/server`), `version`, `description`, and `remotes`, one entry per endpoint with
`type` (`streamable-http`) and `url`. List it in `/.well-known/ai-catalog.json` as an entry of type
`application/mcp-server-card+json` with the card's `url`. A card at `/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json`
is the legacy SEP-1649 shape: it still passes, and SEP-2127 is the shape to publish.

well-known-mcp-card.title: A .well-known MCP server card is published
well-known-mcp-card.goal: Publish a SEP-2127 server card for your MCP server and list it in your AI catalog
well-known-mcp-card.fix:
This check is retired in favor of `mcp-server-card`, which scores the server card. Serve a SEP-2127 card at
`<endpoint>/server-card` carrying `$schema`, `name`, `version`, `description`, and `remotes` (each
with `type` and `url`), and list it in `/.well-known/ai-catalog.json`. The SEP-1649 path,
`/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json`, is the legacy location.

mcp-card-legacy-aliases.title: Legacy MCP card paths redirect to the canonical card
mcp-card-legacy-aliases.goal: Point every legacy MCP card path at the canonical card instead of serving its own copy
mcp-card-legacy-aliases.fix:
Serve whichever legacy pointer paths you publish (`/.well-known/mcp`, `/.well-known/mcp.json`,
`/mcp.json`) as `301` redirects to `/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json`. A legacy path that
answers with its own JSON body is a second source of truth that may drift from the canonical
card, and a `302`/`307` or a redirect to any other location sends agents somewhere else.
Paths you never published need no redirect.

mcp-usage-doc.title: A human/agent usage doc for the server resolves
mcp-usage-doc.goal: Publish a one-fetch markdown usage doc for your MCP server
mcp-usage-doc.fix:
Link a short markdown usage doc for your MCP server (curl examples, the tool list, auth, and
rate limits) at a stable path such as `/mcp-skill.md`, `/mcp.md`, or `/.well-known/mcp/usage.md`,
and reference it from the server card and `llms.txt`. It gives an agent a one-fetch orientation.

mcp-auth-challenge.title: a 401 names the RFC 9728 metadata in its WWW-Authenticate challenge
mcp-auth-challenge.goal: Name your protected-resource metadata in the WWW-Authenticate challenge of every 401
mcp-auth-challenge.fix:
When the MCP endpoint refuses a request that carries no access token, answer `401` with
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://<host>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"`,
naming the URL of your RFC 9728 metadata. A client reads the challenge to find the authorization
server; without `resource_metadata` it falls back to guessing well-known locations. The MCP
authorization specification requires the header on every `401`.

mcp-auth-servers.title: protected-resource metadata lists public https authorization_servers
mcp-auth-servers.goal: List the authorization servers that issue tokens for your MCP server in its RFC 9728 metadata
mcp-auth-servers.fix:
Publish `authorization_servers` in your protected-resource metadata as an array of at least one
issuer URL. Each entry must be an absolute `https` URL on a public host, because a client fetches
that authorization server's own metadata to begin the OAuth flow. A private, loopback, or `http`
URL leaves every client outside your network unable to sign in.

mcp-auth-enforced.title: a tools/list without an access token is refused with 401
mcp-auth-enforced.goal: Refuse every MCP request that carries no access token with 401
mcp-auth-enforced.fix:
Check the access token before dispatching any JSON-RPC method, `tools/list` included, and answer a
request without one with `401` and the same `WWW-Authenticate` challenge `initialize` receives. A
server that challenges some methods but serves `tools/list` to anyone exposes its tool catalog to
callers that never signed in, and leaves a client unable to tell which calls need a token.

llms-txt.title: /llms.txt present with a summary and link index
llms-txt.goal: Serve /llms.txt with a title, summary, and categorized link index
llms-txt.fix:
Serve `/llms.txt` (llmstxt.org): an H1 title, a one-line summary blockquote, and a categorized
index of links to your most important pages as markdown. It is the canonical entry point an
agent fetches to understand what a site offers and where to look next.

llms-full-txt.title: /llms-full.txt present
llms-full-txt.goal: Serve the whole docs corpus as markdown at /llms-full.txt for one-fetch ingestion
llms-full-txt.fix:
For a docs site, concatenate every page as markdown at `/llms-full.txt` so an agent can ingest
the whole corpus in one fetch instead of crawling. Keep it generated from source so it never
drifts from the live pages.

llms-txt-scoped.title: Per-section llms.txt files resolve
llms-txt-scoped.goal: Serve a scoped llms.txt inside each major content section
llms-txt-scoped.fix:
Serve a scoped `llms.txt` inside each major content section linked from your root index (for
example `/docs/llms.txt`). A section-scoped index lets an agent working inside that section
orient itself without re-reading the whole site index.

llms-full-txt-scoped.title: Per-section llms-full.txt files resolve
llms-full-txt-scoped.goal: Serve a scoped llms-full.txt corpus inside each major content section
llms-full-txt-scoped.fix:
Serve a scoped `llms-full.txt` inside each major content section (for example
`/docs/llms-full.txt`): the section's pages concatenated as markdown. An agent can then ingest
one section in one fetch instead of crawling it.

openapi.title: An OpenAPI description is published
openapi.goal: Publish an OpenAPI description so non-MCP agents can call your HTTP API
openapi.fix:
If your service exposes an HTTP/REST API (separate from any MCP endpoint), publish an OpenAPI
3.1 description of it at `/openapi.json` (or `/openapi.yaml`, or `/.well-known/openapi.json`).
When your `/.well-known/api-catalog` lists API anchors, the description scored is the one each
anchor's `service-desc` links to, wherever it is hosted, not these paths: publish it at that URL.
Non-MCP agents use it to discover endpoints, parameters, and response shapes, and to generate
typed clients. A service whose only machine surface is MCP has no REST API to describe here.

json-schemas.title: Referenced JSON Schemas resolve
json-schemas.goal: Serve the JSON Schemas your API references so agents can validate payloads pre-flight
json-schemas.fix:
Serve the input and output JSON Schemas your API references (for example
`/api/schema/input.json`) as `application/schema+json`. Agents validate payloads against them
before calling, which turns a class of runtime failures into pre-flight validation.

accept-markdown.title: Accept text/markdown returns markdown
accept-markdown.goal: Honor Accept text/markdown on content URLs with raw markdown, not HTML chrome
accept-markdown.fix:
Honor `Accept: text/markdown` on content URLs and return raw markdown rather than HTML chrome.
Agents parse markdown far more reliably than a JS-rendered page. Serve the markdown twin at the
same URL via content negotiation, invisibly to crawlers.

markdown-cli-ua.title: Bare CLI User-Agent receives the markdown twin
markdown-cli-ua.goal: Serve the markdown twin to shell HTTP clients that state no content-type preference
markdown-cli-ua.fix:
Sniff the request User-Agent and serve the markdown twin to bare shell clients (`curl`, `wget`,
and language HTTP libraries) that send `Accept: */*` or no `Accept` at all. A scripted `curl
https://your.site/` should get the raw markdown source, not the HTML shell, so pipelines parse
content instead of scraping chrome. Return the same twin you already expose to
`Accept: text/markdown`, keyed on the User-Agent this time.

markdown-agent-ua.title: AI user-fetch User-Agent receives the markdown twin
markdown-agent-ua.goal: Serve the markdown twin to AI on-demand user-fetchers that state no content-type preference
markdown-agent-ua.fix:
Recognize the AI on-demand user-fetch User-Agents (`ChatGPT-User`, `Claude-User`,
`Perplexity-User`) and serve them the markdown twin when they send `Accept: */*` or no `Accept`.
These fetchers retrieve a page on a person's behalf and parse markdown far more reliably than a
JS-rendered page, so handing them source improves what the assistant reads back. Match the token
case-insensitively and fall through to HTML for everything you do not recognize.

markdown-accept-plain.title: Accept text/plain returns the markdown twin
markdown-accept-plain.goal: Treat Accept text/plain as a request for the raw markdown source
markdown-accept-plain.fix:
Treat `Accept: text/plain` as a markdown request and return the raw markdown source rather than
the HTML shell. Many clients and libraries default to `text/plain` when they want the bytes, not
a rendered document, so honoring it hands them the same twin you serve for `Accept:
text/markdown`. Set the response `Content-Type` to `text/markdown` (or `text/plain`) so the
negotiated content type is unambiguous.

markdown-vary.title: Negotiated responses carry Vary Accept
markdown-vary.goal: Name every negotiated request header in Vary so shared caches never serve one client the wrong variant
markdown-vary.fix:
When the same URL serves HTML or markdown depending on the request, emit a `Vary` header on
every response that names each request header the choice depends on: `Vary: Accept` when you
negotiate on `Accept` alone, and `Vary: Accept, User-Agent` when agent User-Agents also receive
the markdown twin. Without it a shared cache (a CDN or a corporate proxy) can store the markdown
twin under the bare URL and then hand it to a browser, or the reverse. If the CDN ignores or
strips Vary (Cloudflare's zone cache historically keeps only `Accept-Encoding`), do not give
that cache a long `s-maxage` on negotiated responses: HIT replies would then reach clients with
no Vary, and the check still fails.

markdown-frontmatter.title: Markdown twin carries YAML frontmatter
markdown-frontmatter.goal: Prefix the markdown twin with a YAML frontmatter block so agents read page metadata without parsing the body
markdown-frontmatter.fix:
Open each markdown twin with a YAML frontmatter block: a `---` fence line, `title`, `description`, and a
canonical `url` key, then a closing `---` fence, before the first heading. An agent then lifts the page's
title, summary, and canonical URL from structured keys instead of inferring them from prose, which is both
cheaper and less error-prone. Keep the block well-formed: an opened fence with no terminator, or a fence pair
with no keys, is worse than no frontmatter because it misleads a parser.

root-meta-description.title: Root HTML has a descriptive meta description
root-meta-description.goal: Add a meta description naming what the service does and its agent entry points
root-meta-description.fix:
Add a `<meta name="description">` to your root HTML that states what the service does and names
its agent entry points (MCP endpoint, `llms.txt`, OpenAPI). It is the cheapest machine-readable
summary and it feeds link previews and search snippets too.

root-link-rel.title: Root HTML links to machine surfaces via link rel
root-link-rel.goal: Point link rel elements at your machine surfaces from the root HTML head
root-link-rel.fix:
Add `<link rel>` elements in your root HTML head pointing at your machine surfaces:
`rel="service-desc"` to the OpenAPI doc, `rel="service-doc"` to human docs, and
`rel="alternate"` to `llms.txt` and the MCP card. An agent that lands on the HTML can then
discover the structured surfaces without scraping.

noscript-fallback.title: Root HTML has a noscript with machine entry points
noscript-fallback.goal: Give non-JS agents a noscript block listing your machine entry points
noscript-fallback.fix:
Add a `<noscript>` block to your root HTML that links your machine entry points: `llms.txt`,
your OpenAPI or MCP endpoint, and any `.well-known` cards. It hands a fetch-only crawler or a
non-JS agent a concrete, in-body list of where the structured surfaces live, so it never has to
run the client bundle or infer them from the visible page.

schema-org-jsonld.title: Root HTML embeds Schema.org JSON-LD
schema-org-jsonld.goal: Embed Schema.org JSON-LD so agents get typed facts without inference
schema-org-jsonld.fix:
Embed Schema.org JSON-LD (for example `TechArticle`, `WebAPI`, or `SoftwareApplication`) in a
`<script type="application/ld+json">` in your head. Structured metadata gives agents and search
engines typed facts about the page without inference.

semantic-html.title: Root HTML uses semantic landmarks
semantic-html.goal: Use semantic landmarks so the HTML path is parseable structure, not div soup
semantic-html.fix:
Use `<main>`, `<article>`, `<section>`, and `<nav>` landmarks so the HTML path is parseable.
An agent that has to fall back to reading the DOM should find structure, not a wall of
`<div>`s.

robots.title: /robots.txt present
robots.goal: Publish robots.txt and state your crawl policy explicitly
robots.fix:
Publish a `robots.txt`. Declare your crawl and AI-usage policy explicitly rather than leaving
it to inference. An absent `robots.txt` is ambiguous; a present one is a clear signal.

sitemap.title: /sitemap.xml present
sitemap.goal: Publish sitemap.xml so agents can enumerate your content URLs
sitemap.fix:
Publish a `sitemap.xml` so crawlers and agents can enumerate your content URLs instead of
discovering them by following links. Keep it generated so it stays current.

robots-ai-rules.title: robots.txt declares AI-crawler rules
robots-ai-rules.goal: State your AI-crawler policy in robots.txt with explicit User-agent rules
robots-ai-rules.fix:
Add explicit `User-agent` rules for AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended,
PerplexityBot, CCBot, and others) to `robots.txt`, or a wildcard policy. Stating your stance
(RFC 9309) removes ambiguity about whether AI systems may fetch your content.

content-signals.title: robots.txt declares Content-Signal preferences
content-signals.goal: Declare Content-Signal AI-usage preferences in robots.txt
content-signals.fix:
Add `Content-Signal` directives to `robots.txt` (contentsignals.org): `ai-train`, `search`,
and `ai-input` set to `yes` or `no`. They express usage preferences at a finer grain than a
blanket allow/deny.

security-txt.title: /.well-known/security.txt present
security-txt.goal: Publish security.txt with a Contact and Expires field
security-txt.fix:
Publish `/.well-known/security.txt` (RFC 9116) with a `Contact` and an `Expires` field so a
researcher or agent can find how to report a problem. It is a small, standard trust signal.

web-bot-auth.title: Web Bot Auth signature directory present
web-bot-auth.goal: Publish an HTTP Message Signatures directory if your site sends signed bot traffic
web-bot-auth.fix:
Informational only. If your site sends authenticated bot traffic, publish an HTTP Message
Signatures JWKS directory at `/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory` so recipients can
verify your bot's signatures. Skip it if you do not send signed bot requests.

link-headers.title: Homepage sends RFC 8288 Link headers
link-headers.goal: Advertise machine surfaces in a Link response header on / for header-only discovery
link-headers.fix:
Send a `Link` response header on `/` (RFC 8288) whose `rel` points at your machine surfaces, so an
agent reading only response headers finds them without parsing HTML or probing `/.well-known`. Use
the RFC 8631 service trio and the RFC 9727 catalog: `rel="service-desc"` at a machine-readable
description (OpenAPI, or an MCP server card), `rel="service-doc"` at the human-readable doc,
`rel="service-meta"` at the service-context declaration, and `rel="api-catalog"` at your
`/.well-known/api-catalog` index. Example:
`Link: </.well-known/api-catalog>; rel="api-catalog", </.well-known/mcp/server-card.json>; rel="service-desc"`.

api-catalog.title: /.well-known/api-catalog published
api-catalog.goal: Serve an RFC 9727 api-catalog linkset indexing your API descriptions
api-catalog.fix:
Serve `/.well-known/api-catalog` (RFC 9727) as `application/linkset+json` with a `linkset[]` of
anchor plus `service-desc` entries. It is the standard index that points agents at every API
description you publish.

json-errors.title: API client errors return JSON, not HTML
json-errors.goal: Return a JSON error body on client-error API responses so agents can parse the failure
json-errors.fix:
On a client-error API response (4xx), return `Content-Type: application/json` and a JSON object
(for example `{ "error": { "code": "not_found", "message": "..." } }`), not an HTML error page.
Agents cannot recover from a soft-HTML 404. The audit probes a documented OpenAPI 4xx GET when
one exists, otherwise `GET /anc-web-audit-no-such-api`.

rate-limit-headers.title: API responses advertise rate-limit headers
rate-limit-headers.goal: Advertise remaining quota on API responses so agents can back off instead of retrying blindly
rate-limit-headers.fix:
Send IETF RateLimit headers (`RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, `RateLimit-Reset`) or
the common `X-RateLimit-*` aliases on API responses. A 429 should also carry `Retry-After`.
Without them an agent has no budget and will retry until it is locked out.

a2a-agent-card.title: A2A Agent Card published
a2a-agent-card.goal: Publish an A2A Agent Card for agent-to-agent discovery
a2a-agent-card.fix:
Serve an A2A Agent Card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` (a2a-protocol.org) with `name`,
`version`, and `supportedInterfaces`. It lets other agents discover and interoperate with yours
over the agent-to-agent protocol.

ai-catalog.title: /.well-known/ai-catalog.json published
ai-catalog.goal: Publish an Agentic Resource Discovery catalog so agents can enumerate your AI artifacts
ai-catalog.fix:
Serve `/.well-known/ai-catalog.json` as JSON with `specVersion` and an `entries` array (the
AI Catalog / ARD envelope). Each entry should identify an artifact (`identifier`, `type`, and
a `url` or inline `data`). Missing the file is fine (this check is MAY); a 200 that is not a
catalog is worse than absence.

agent-skills.title: Agent-skills discovery index published
agent-skills.goal: Publish an agent-skills discovery index so agents can enumerate your skills
agent-skills.fix:
Publish an agent-skills discovery index at `/.well-known/agent-skills/index.json` (the
Cloudflare agent-skills-discovery draft) with a `skills[]` array, so agents can enumerate the
skills your site exposes.

dns-aid.title: DNS-AID records under _agents
dns-aid.goal: Publish DNSSEC-signed SVCB records under _agents for DNS-level agent discovery
dns-aid.fix:
Publish SVCB/HTTPS records under the `_agents` namespace (for example
`_index._agents.<domain>`, `_mcp._agents.<domain>`), DNSSEC-signed
(draft-mozleywilliams-dnsop-dnsaid). DNS-level discovery lets an agent find your endpoints
before any HTTP request.

oauth-discovery.title: OAuth/OIDC discovery metadata published
oauth-discovery.goal: Publish OAuth/OIDC discovery metadata if agents authenticate to your service
oauth-discovery.fix:
If agents authenticate to your service, publish OAuth/OIDC discovery metadata at
`/.well-known/openid-configuration` or `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` (RFC 8414 /
OIDC Discovery). Absent metadata is expected for an open server; present metadata is required
for an authenticated one.

oauth-protected-resource.title: OAuth Protected Resource Metadata published
oauth-protected-resource.goal: Publish RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata for your authenticated MCP server
oauth-protected-resource.fix:
For an authenticated MCP server, publish `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` (RFC 9728) so
a client can discover which authorization servers issue tokens for your resource. Expected
absent for an open, no-auth server.

auth-md.title: Agent auth/registration metadata doc published
auth-md.goal: Publish an auth.md telling agents how to obtain credentials
auth-md.fix:
Publish an `auth.md` at `/.well-known/auth.md` (or `/auth.md`): a short markdown guide that
tells an agent how to obtain credentials, including where to register, which OAuth flows are
supported, token endpoints, and scopes. It turns "figure out our auth" into a one-fetch
orientation.

webmcp.title: Root HTML exposes WebMCP browser tools
webmcp.goal: Expose page tools to browser agents via WebMCP
webmcp.fix:
Expose page functionality to browser agents via WebMCP: register a `navigator.modelContext`
provider or declare tools in a `<script type="application/webmcp+json">` block. In-page tools
let a browser-hosted agent act on the page without scraping the DOM.

agent-friendly-404.title: Unknown paths return HTTP 404 or 410
agent-friendly-404.goal: Return a real HTTP 404 or 410 for unknown paths instead of a 200 SPA shell
agent-friendly-404.fix:
Configure the origin so a nonsense path under the site returns HTTP 404 or 410, not 200 with
the application shell. A soft-404 hides recovery from agents: they treat the page as content
and never look for a sitemap or `llms.txt`. Verify with
`curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://example.com/this-path-does-not-exist` — it
MUST print `404` (or `410`).

agent-friendly-404-md.title: 404 body is markdown with a recovery link
agent-friendly-404-md.goal: Serve a short markdown 404 that links at least one agent recovery surface
agent-friendly-404-md.fix:
When `Accept: text/markdown` hits an unknown path, return 404 or 410 with a short markdown
body that includes at least one recovery link: sitemap, `llms.txt`, a docs index, or an
equivalent same-origin href. Linking both sitemap and `llms.txt` as absolute URLs is the
stronger pattern. Zero links is a miss even when the status is correct.

content-without-js.title: Root HTML has an H1 and readable text without JavaScript
content-without-js.goal: Put an H1 and enough visible text in the raw root HTML that a non-JS agent can read the page
content-without-js.fix:
Render an `<h1>` and at least about 200 characters of visible text in the raw HTML of `/` so
a client that does not execute JavaScript still gets a page. A thin SPA shell is acceptable
only when `/llms.txt` is present and links resolvable same-origin content (the audit then
marks this check not applicable, not a pass). Dead `llms.txt` links do not soften the floor.

agent-ua-reachable.title: AI user-fetch User-Agent can reach the homepage
agent-ua-reachable.goal: Let on-demand user-fetchers GET / with Accept */* and receive 2xx, not a challenge page
agent-ua-reachable.fix:
Allow AI user-fetch clients such as `ChatGPT-User` to `GET /` with `Accept: */*` and receive
a 2xx response whose body is not an obvious bot-challenge interstitial. This is reachability,
not content type: serving HTML is fine. Blocklists that 403 these UAs, or challenge pages that
say "Just a moment", fail the check.

llms-txt-format.title: llms.txt has H1, summary, and a link index
llms-txt-format.goal: Structure /llms.txt with an H1, a blockquote summary, and a markdown link index
llms-txt-format.fix:
Follow the llmstxt.org shape: start with `# Title`, add a `>` summary blockquote, then a
categorized list of markdown links. A file that is present but is only a heading, or only a
blob of prose, fails this row even when the presence check passes.

llms-txt-links.title: llms.txt links resolve
llms-txt-links.goal: Make every markdown href in /llms.txt https and fetchable
llms-txt-links.fix:
Probe the markdown links in `/llms.txt` and replace 404s. An agent that follows a dead index
link wastes a round-trip and may conclude the project has no docs. Write every link as an
`https` URL that answers over https without redirecting to `http`: an `http` link, or one
that redirects to `http`, is never requested and reads noncompliant. Keep the list short
and current; drop links you are not willing to keep alive.

llms-txt-when-to-use.title: llms.txt has a when-to-use or programmatic-access section
llms-txt-when-to-use.goal: Tell agents when to use the MCP or docs from a short llms.txt heading
llms-txt-when-to-use.fix:
Add a heading such as `## When to use` or `## Programmatic access` with a few lines on when
an agent should connect (for example: "Use the MCP when you need to search or score a CLI").
The audit looks for that heading; it does not grade the prose with an LLM.
